catalog_quote: [p.469] Fatamanue has five vowels with short versus long /i,e,a,o,u/ and sixteen consonants /p,t,k,b,d,g,f,s,h,m,n,ng,r,l,w,y/. Word stress is phonemic. [...] [p.471] Fatamanue has two stress patterns as seen in some languages of Maluku. The majority of words are stressed on the penultimate syllable. Some stress falls on the final. But, the stress remains in its original position, even when plural or other suffixes are added. This stress pattern is similar to the Big Nambas's of Vanuatu (Fox 1979). new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress is lexically contrastive between penultimate (the majority pattern) and final syllable of the stem, with minimal pairs; stress is a property of the stem and does not move when plural or possessive/other suffixes are added (so suffixed penult-stressed stems surface with antepenultimate stress, e.g. aí-u 'my foot' vs u-ái 'my tree').
new_statements.exceptions: Final-stressed stems are a lexical minority, marked with an acute in the noun lists (p.474: 'stems having stress on the final are indicated only for the singular'); author regards phonemic stress as a secondary development, possibly substrate-influenced.
new_statements.domain_note: Word/stem level; stress fixed on the stem under suffixation. Description is primarily of the Haruru dialect; Yalahatan differs slightly (f > h in some words).
new_statements.identity_note: Sakiyama's 'Fatamanue' = Atamanu, the language of Desa Haruru and Desa Yalahatan (plus extinct Awaiya), i.e. exactly Glottolog yala1266 Yalahatan-Haruru-Awaiya (iso jal). The description is 'primarily concerned with the Haruru dialect'; Yalahatan shows slight dialect variation (some f > h) but the stress statement is given for the language as a whole.
